Task 4
The following code creates a new column in both data frames called status.

bp_list$treatment$status <- character(20)
bp_list$placebo$status <- character(10)

The following code creates the new status column’s values using a for loop in the placebo data frame.

for (i in 1:20) {
  
  if (bp_list$treatment$post_bp[i] <= 120) {
    bp_list$treatment$status[i] <- "optimal"
    
  } else if (bp_list$treatment$post_bp[i] <= 130) {
    bp_list$treatment$status[i] <- "borderline"
    
  } else {
    bp_list$treatment$status[i] <- "high"
  }
}

The following code does the same thing as the above block but for the non-placebo data frame.

for (i in 1:10) {
  
  if (bp_list$placebo$post_bp[i] <= 120) {
    bp_list$placebo$status[i] <- "optimal"
    
  } else if (bp_list$placebo$post_bp[i] <= 130) {
    bp_list$placebo$status[i] <- "borderline"
    
  } else {
    bp_list$placebo$status[i] <- "high"
  }
}

Task 1

I would use this path ../MyData.csv.
The major benefits of using R projects include:


R projects keeps all my different project file types in one folder.
R projects is integrated with tools like Git so I can easily use the terminal to upload and share my work.
R projects provides a nice UI to keep up with all my project files and data in one place.


Git is a version control tool that allows you to track changes in your code on your computer. Github, on the other hand, is a website that allows you to upload these changes to share with others. You can also download (pull) other Github users’ code.
A tibble doesn’t show the entire dataset like a dataframe would when you print it, and it rather shows only rows that fit on the screen. When you access one column of a tibble, it will keep the tibble structure, but when you access one column of a dataframe, it will become a vector.

getIQR <- function(x, ...) {

title: Homework 9
text:
Standardize the weather predictors
For each weather predictor, we subtract its training mean and divide by its training standard deviation.
The test data must use the same training means and standard deviations, which prevents test set information from influencing preprocessing.
We keep the original variables and create standardized versions with the ending _z. We don’t need to standardize the rental count.

weather_vars <- c(
  "temp", "humidity", "wind_speed", "visibility",
  "dew_point", "solar_radiation", "rainfall", "snowfall"
)

training_means <- sapply(train[weather_vars], mean)
training_sds <- sapply(train[weather_vars], sd)

# Standardization requires nonzero standard deviations.
stopifnot(all(training_sds > 0))

for (variable in weather_vars) {
  new_name <- paste0(variable, "_z")

  train[[new_name]] <- (
    train[[variable]] - training_means[[variable]]
  ) / training_sds[[variable]]

  test[[new_name]] <- (
    test[[variable]] - training_means[[variable]]
  ) / training_sds[[variable]]
}

Compare test-set RMSE

text:
Refit the selected model using all daily observations
After selecting model 3, we refit it using the entire daily data set. We now calculate standardization means and standard deviations from all daily observations.
The earlier test RMSE belongs to the model trained on the training set. It is not an independent evaluation of this final model, which uses all observations.

full_data <- daily |>
  mutate(
    day_type = factor(
      if_else(
        wday(date, week_start = 1) >= 6,
        "Weekend",
        "Weekday"
      ),
      levels = c("Weekday", "Weekend")
    )
  )

full_means <- sapply(full_data[weather_vars], mean)
full_sds <- sapply(full_data[weather_vars], sd)

stopifnot(all(full_sds > 0))

for (variable in weather_vars) {
  new_name <- paste0(variable, "_z")

  full_data[[new_name]] <- (
    full_data[[variable]] - full_means[[variable]]
  ) / full_sds[[variable]]
}

models <- list(model1, model2, model3)
best_formula <- formula(models[[best_index]])

best_formula

bike_count ~ temp_z + humidity_z + wind_speed_z + visibility_z + 
    dew_point_z + solar_radiation_z + rainfall_z + snowfall_z + 
    seasons + holiday + day_type + I(temp_z^2) + I(humidity_z^2) + 
    seasons:holiday + temp_z:seasons + temp_z:rainfall_z

final_model <- lm(
  best_formula,
  data = full_data
)
